name: Kingdom of Ife
info: The Yoruba holy city of Ilé-Ifẹ̀, ruled by the Ooni, whose naturalistic bronze, stone and terracotta sculptures of 1200–1400 and its glass-bead industry made it the sacred and artistic centre of Yorubaland.

facts.founder: Oduduwa, who created a dynasty at Ife in Yoruba tradition; the city itself was founded by Obatala at the order of Olodumare, by the same traditions
facts.predecessor: The pre-urban confederation of sixteen clans of early Ife, the Elu Merindinlogun
facts.successor: British colonial rule; the Ooni of Ife continues as a traditional ruler in Osun State, Nigeria

t: In Yoruba religion Oduduwa descended on a chain, cast earth on the primordial ocean and founded Ilé-Ifẹ̀ as the first city; his sons, daughters and grandchildren went out to found Ila Orangun, Owu, Ketu, Sabe, Egba, Popo, Ijesha and Oyo, and his son Oranmiyan the second dynasty of Benin.

Between 1200 and 1400 the artists of Ife made naturalistic sculptures in terracotta, stone and copper alloy, many under the patronage of King Obalufon II, honoured as the inventor of bronze casting in a life-size copper mask.

The sacred grove of Igbo Olokun held one of the earliest known glass workshops in West Africa, at its peak from the eleventh to the fifteenth century; its high-lime, high-alumina beads have been found at Igbo-Ukwu, Gao, Essouk and Kissi.
dyk: Ife is called the city of 401 deities: the Ooni is counted the 401st orisha, the only one that speaks, and traditional worshippers are said to celebrate a festival of one deity on every day of the year.
ev: By 900 Ifẹ̀, founded between 1000 and 500 BCE, has become an important West African emporium producing sophisticated art.
Glass production is under way at the sacred grove of Igbo Olokun, if it has not begun earlier; the eleventh to fifteenth centuries are its peak.
From the twelfth to the fourteenth century the city is a settlement of substantial size, its houses laid with potsherd pavements.
The artists of Ife develop a refined naturalistic tradition in terracotta, stone and copper alloy, much of it under King Obalufon II.
After 1400 production of the sculptures declines as political and economic power shifts to the neighbouring kingdom of Benin, which, like Oyo, grows into a major empire.
The distinct Yoruba glassmaking technology persists in the Osun Grove into the seventeenth century.
In the mid-nineteenth century the Oyo Empire, founded from Ife by Oranmiyan and stretching at its height from the Niger to the Volta, collapses.

sections.foundation:
Ilé-Ifẹ̀ is an ancient Yoruba city in south-western Nigeria, founded at some time between 1000 and 500 BCE; by 900 CE it had become an important West African emporium producing sophisticated art. Its own account of its origin is the Yoruba story of the creation of the world. Olodumare, the Supreme God, ordered Obatala to create the earth, but Obatala drank too much palm wine on the way, and the orisha Oduduwa took the items of creation from him, descended from the abode of the orisha on a chain and cast a handful of earth on the primordial ocean. The earth rose as a mound, Oke Ora; a five-toed cockerel scattered it to make the land on which the first city would be built, and a palm nut Oduduwa planted sprang up as a tree with sixteen branches, the sixteen clans of the early Ife pre-urban confederation, the Elu Merindinlogun.

The name Ife means 'expansion', and Ile-Ife 'the land', or in modern Yoruba 'the home', 'of expansion'. Oduduwa's usurpation of creation began an everlasting rivalry with Obatala, which the votaries of the two divinities still re-enact at the Itapa New Year festival; Oduduwa became the ancestor of the first divine king of the Yoruba, and Obatala is believed to have made the first Yoruba people from clay. Oduduwa created a dynasty at Ife, and the first Ooni was his descendant. The Ooni is traditionally counted the 401st orisha, the only one that speaks, and the royal dynasty traces its origin to the founding of the city.
sections.socioeconomy:
Agriculture occupied most of Ife's people, and the region still produces vegetables, grain, cocoa, tobacco and cotton. Between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries the city was a settlement of substantial size, its houses laid with potsherd pavements. Iron was smelted in the Ife region: excavations at Iyekere have found burnt tuyères, stone tools, decorated potsherds, charcoal and slag, and the smelting was efficient, working ore of nearly 80 per cent iron oxide and leaving a lean slag.

The city's most far-reaching industry was glass. In the sacred grove of Igbo Olokun, where the goddess Olokun was worshipped, glass beads and production materials have been excavated, and analysis dates the main working to the eleventh to fifteenth centuries, perhaps beginning earlier; it may be one of the earliest glass workshops in West Africa, and its recipes, raw materials and pyrotechnology were largely independent of traditions farther afield. Two compositions, high-lime high-alumina and low-lime high-alumina glass, were developed from local materials. Beads of the first kind found at Igbo-Ukwu in southern Nigeria, at Gao and Essouk in Mali and at Kissi in Burkina Faso after the ninth century show the industry's part in regional trade, including the trans-Saharan trade. In the Osun Grove the technology persisted into the seventeenth century.
sections.military:
The sources for Ife say little of war; the city's power was spiritual and dynastic, and its reach was carried by its princes rather than its armies. In tradition the Ooni was head of the spiritual, political and military affairs of all the lands before the other kingdoms went out from Ife to establish their own territories, and every other Yoruba ruler is called igbakeji orisha, second to the orisha who is the Ooni. The dispersal from the holy city was the kingdom's expansion. Oduduwa's sons, daughters and grandchildren founded their own kingdoms and empires: Ila Orangun, Owu, Ketu, Sabe, Egba, Popo, Ijesha and Oyo.

Oranmiyan, Oduduwa's last-born and one of his father's principal ministers, was sent to govern the nascent Edo kingdom when its people asked for Oduduwa's rule. When he returned to Ile-Ife after a period of service in Benin he left behind Eweka, his son by Erinmwinde, daughter of the Ogie of Egor, who became the first widely accepted Oba of the second Edo dynasty that has ruled Benin ever since. Oranmiyan then went north-west into the savanna to found Oyo, which grew into an empire stretching at its height from the right bank of the Niger to the left bank of the Volta, one of the most powerful of Africa's medieval states until its collapse in the mid-nineteenth century. Those two creations of Ife's dynasty, Benin and Oyo, became the military powers of the region, and after 1400 political and economic power passed from Ife to them.
sections.governance:
Ife was ruled by the Ooni, the title of the god-king Oduduwa, which every king of Ife took after his reign. The Ooni was the spiritual and political leader of the people later called Yoruba and the head of spiritual, political and military affairs across all the lands before the other kingdoms were founded; he is counted the 401st orisha, and all other Yoruba kings are 'igbakeji orisha', second in command to him. He is the chief priest and custodian of the holy city of all the Yoruba. Historically the king appeared in public only once a year, at the Olojo festival, the celebration of the new dawn.

Religion was the frame of rule. Ife is called the city of 401 deities, irunmole or orisha, and a festival of one of them is said to fall on every day of the year, often extending over several days and joining priestly rites in the palace to theatrical dramatisations in the rest of the kingdom: the Itapa festival for Obatala and Obameri, the Edi festival for Moremi Ajasoro, the Ugbo with their Igare masqueraders. Shrines and groves held the cults: the Oduduwa Shrine and Grove of the progenitor of the Yoruba, the Agbonniregun Temple of Orunmila, orisha of wisdom and divination, and Igbo Olokun. In art, kings and gods were shown with large heads because the ase, a person's inner power, was believed to be held there, and both historic figures and the offices they held were represented.
sections.impact:
Ife is the holy city of the Yoruba and the source of their royal lines. By its traditions the dynasties of Ila Orangun, Owu, Ketu, Sabe, Egba, Popo, Ijesha and Oyo descend from Oduduwa, and through Oranmiyan's son Eweka the second dynasty of Benin as well; Oyo became one of the most powerful of Africa's medieval states, and Benin a major empire. The Ooni is regarded as chief priest and custodian of the holy city of all the Yoruba, and since the Yoruba Orisha Congress of 1986 he has held an international standing the title had not had since the city's colonisation by the British.

Ife's art is its lasting mark on the world. Its naturalistic bronze, stone and terracotta sculptures, which reached their peak between 1200 and 1400, are significant examples of naturalism in pre-colonial African art, distinguished by their regalia, facial marking patterns and body proportions; the life-size copper mask of King Obalufon II, honoured as the Yoruba patron deity of brass casting, weaving and regalia, is the best documented. Its glass beads travelled farther still, to Igbo-Ukwu, to Gao and Essouk in Mali, to Kissi in Burkina Faso, to Mauritania and Ghana, as a currency of power and belief for Yoruba, West Africans and, in time, the African diaspora. The city is now home to the Obafemi Awolowo University and Oduduwa University, and remains, as the city of 401 deities, the place where the orisha are celebrated through the year.
sections.decline:
Ife's eminence as a centre of power did not outlast its art. After the sculptural tradition peaked between 1200 and 1400, production declined as political and economic power shifted to the nearby kingdom of Benin, which, like the Yoruba kingdom of Oyo, developed into a major empire. Both were in tradition the creations of Ife's own dynasty, and both outgrew it: Oyo at its height stretched from the Niger to the Volta before it collapsed in the mid-nineteenth century. The glass industry of Igbo Olokun passed its peak in the fifteenth century, though the distinct Yoruba technology persisted in the Osun Grove into the seventeenth. Ife kept what the empires could not take, the sacred standing of the Ooni and the cults of its 401 deities.

The city was colonised by the British, after which the holders of the Ooni's title lost the wider standing they would regain only in 1986 with the Yoruba Orisha Congress. The throne itself continued: Adesoji Aderemi, Atobatele I (1889–1980), was the 49th Ooni; Okunade Sijuwade, Olubuse II (1930–2015), the 50th; and since 2015 Adeyeye Enitan Ogunwusi, Ojaja II, a Nigerian accountant born in 1974, has reigned as the 51st. Today Ife is a city of more than 500,000 people, the largest in Osun State by the 2006 census, divided between the Ife East and Ife Central local government areas; the Ooni is prominent among Nigeria's royal obas, and the festivals of the orisha continue.

summary: Ilé-Ifẹ̀ is the holy city of the Yoruba, where Oduduwa founded the dynasty from which Oyo, Benin and the other Yoruba kingdoms claim descent. Ruled by the Ooni, it produced between 1200 and 1400 the naturalistic bronze, stone and terracotta sculptures and the glass beads for which it is famous, before power passed to Benin and Oyo.
references: Frank Willett, Ife in the History of West African Sculpture (Thames & Hudson, 1967)
Suzanne Preston Blier, Art and Risk in Ancient Yoruba: Ife History, Power, and Identity, c. 1300 (Cambridge University Press, 2015)

pointDescs.1000: Ife, an important West African emporium by 900, enters the second millennium as a city producing sophisticated art under the dynasty of Oduduwa.
pointDescs.1100: Glass production at Igbo Olokun is under way, if it had not begun earlier; the eleventh century opens its peak period.
pointDescs.1200: The city is a settlement of substantial size with potsherd pavements, and its sculptural tradition is reaching its peak.
pointDescs.1300: Around 1300 the artists of Ife develop their refined naturalistic tradition in terracotta, stone and copper alloy, much of it under King Obalufon II, honoured as inventor of bronze casting.
pointDescs.1400: The peak of Ife art ends; production declines as political and economic power shifts to Benin and Oyo.
pointDescs.1500: Glass working at Igbo Olokun passes the end of its peak period, the fifteenth century; Benin and Oyo are the rising empires of the region.
pointDescs.1650: The distinct Yoruba glassmaking technology persists in the Osun Grove into the seventeenth century, the last in which it is recorded.
pointDescs.1850: Oyo, founded from Ife by Oranmiyan, collapses in the mid-nineteenth century; Ife remains the holy city and the Ooni its chief priest and custodian.
pointDescs.1900: British colonisation, around the turn of the century, ends the Ooni's wider standing, which the title regains only with the Yoruba Orisha Congress of 1986.

notes: The article is about the city; it has no political history of the kingdom between the dynastic traditions and the present. No ruler is dated before the 49th Ooni (1889–1980), no war, treaty or reign is given, and the British colonisation is undated. The sections are built from the traditions, the art history, the archaeology (iron, glass) and the Ooni's office, and the military section says openly that the sources record no wars.

Register dates 1000–1900: the article gives the city's founding as 1000–500 BC and its emporium status by 900; the end of 1900 stands for the undated British colonisation. Both are noted in the pointDescs.

Events: only two are dated by year in the article (Oyo's collapse 'mid 19th century' and the Orisha Congress 1986, outside the span). The ev list therefore uses the article's century dates ('By 900', '11th century', 'c. 1300', 'After 1400', '17th century', 'Mid-19th century').

The article's statement that the dynasty 'traces its origin back to the founding of the city more than ten thousand years before the birth of Jesus Christ' is a tradition and is not repeated as a date.
The founder fact gives both Oduduwa (dynasty) and Obatala (the city, in the creation story), as the article does; the editor may prefer Oduduwa alone.
No references: the article's reference list is empty (external links only).
